summary: Perindopril erbumine is an oral ACE inhibitor prodrug, hydrolysed to the active metabolite perindoprilat, indicated for essential hypertension and for stable coronary artery disease to reduce cardiovascular mortality or nonfatal MI. For hypertension the usual start is 4 mg once daily (maintenance 4-8 mg, max 16 mg/day); for stable CAD, 4 mg once daily for 2 weeks then 8 mg/day as tolerated. It carries a BOXED WARNING for fetal toxicity and must be stopped when pregnancy is detected. Key class risks are angioedema, hyperkalaemia, hypotension (especially first-dose in volume-depleted patients), cough, and acute renal impairment; it should not be combined with aliskiren in diabetics or with neprilysin inhibitors (sacubitril).

moa: Perindopril erbumine is a prodrug hydrolysed in the liver to perindoprilat, which inhibits angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE, a peptidyl dipeptidase). ACE catalyses conversion of inactive angiotensin I to the potent vasoconstrictor angiotensin II. Inhibition lowers plasma angiotensin II, reducing vasoconstriction and aldosterone secretion (promoting diuresis/natriuresis and a small rise in serum potassium), and increasing plasma renin activity. ACE is also kininase II, so its inhibition raises bradykinin levels, contributing both to vasodilation and to the cough and angioedema seen with ACE inhibitors.

Known hypersensitivity to perindopril or any other ACE inhibitor
Concomitant use with sacubitril (neprilysin inhibitor) or within 36 hours of switching
Co-administration with aliskiren in patients with diabetes

Hyperkalaemia or concomitant potassium-sparing agents/supplements/salt substitutes

preg: BOXED WARNING. Drugs acting on the renin-angiotensin system can cause injury and death to the developing fetus, particularly in the second and third trimesters (oligohydramnios, fetal renal failure, skull hypoplasia, growth restriction, hypotension, death). Discontinue perindopril erbumine as soon as pregnancy is detected and switch to an alternative antihypertensive. If exposure occurs, monitor fetal/neonatal renal function and consider fetal ultrasound.
lact: Limited data; perindopril/perindoprilat passage into human milk is not well characterised. Use is generally not recommended, especially in newborns and preterm infants; an alternative agent with established safety in lactation is preferred. If used, monitor the infant.
renal: Perindoprilat is renally eliminated and accumulates in renal impairment. With CrCl >30 mL/min, standard dosing is usually appropriate. With CrCl <30 mL/min, reduce the dose and titrate cautiously to blood pressure and potassium. Initiation can cause an acute fall in GFR (especially with bilateral renal artery stenosis, volume depletion, or concomitant diuretics/NSAIDs); monitor renal function and potassium closely after starting or increasing the dose.
hepatic: In hepatic impairment, conversion of perindopril to its active metabolite perindoprilat may be reduced. Use with caution; standard dosing is generally tolerated in mild-moderate impairment but the antihypertensive response may be altered.

major: Aliskiren (contraindicated in diabetics; dual RAS blockade - hypotension, hyperkalaemia, renal failure)
Sacubitril/neprilysin inhibitors (contraindicated - angioedema risk; observe 36-h washout)
Potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements, salt substitutes (hyperkalaemia)
Other RAS blockers - ARBs (dual blockade harms)
moderate: NSAIDs including selective COX-2 inhibitors (reduced antihypertensive effect, deterioration of renal function, hyperkalaemia - 'triple whammy' with diuretic)
mTOR inhibitors / DPP-4 inhibitors / NEP inhibitors (increased angioedema risk)
Other antihypertensives and nitrates (additive BP lowering)
interactions.food: Food reduces conversion of perindopril to active perindoprilat - take before a meal and consistently
interactions.alcohol: May enhance the blood-pressure-lowering effect; limit intake
interactions.diagnostics: May raise serum potassium and creatinine; can affect parathyroid testing; consider in renin/aldosterone assessment

serious: Angioedema (face, lips, tongue, glottis, larynx - airway compromise; intestinal angioedema)
Acute renal failure (especially with renal artery stenosis or volume depletion)
rare: Neutropenia / agranulocytosis (especially renal impairment or collagen vascular disease)
Anaphylactoid reactions during dialysis or LDL apheresis
emergency: Angioedema with airway obstruction (stop drug, secure airway, give epinephrine/antihistamine/steroid)
Anaphylactoid reaction during haemodialysis or apheresis

monitoring: Blood pressure (and orthostatic BP), especially after first dose and titration
Serum potassium - at baseline and during treatment
Renal function (serum creatinine, eGFR) at baseline and after initiation/dose change
Watch for angioedema, particularly during the first weeks
CBC if collagen vascular disease and/or renal impairment
Pregnancy status in women of childbearing potential
counsel: If you become pregnant or plan to, stop this medicine and contact your doctor immediately
Report swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or difficulty breathing/swallowing at once (angioedema)
A dry, tickly cough can occur; tell your doctor if it is bothersome (may need a different class)
Stand up slowly to avoid dizziness, especially when starting; the first dose may lower BP markedly
Avoid potassium supplements and salt substitutes unless advised
Avoid regular NSAIDs (ibuprofen, etc.) without medical advice - they reduce effect and harm kidneys
Take before a meal at the same time each day; do not stop suddenly without advice
pk: Blood-pressure lowering begins within ~1 hour; full effect over days-weeks
Perindopril Cmax ~1 h; active perindoprilat peaks ~3-7 h after the dose
Perindopril ~1 h; effective half-life of perindoprilat ~25 h (free perindoprilat); supports once-daily dosing
Store at controlled room temperature; protect from moisture
pearls: BOXED WARNING: stop immediately when pregnancy is detected - RAS-acting drugs cause fetal injury/death.
Prodrug: perindopril is converted to active perindoprilat; food reduces this conversion, so dose before meals.
Do NOT combine with aliskiren in diabetics or with sacubitril (neprilysin inhibitor); allow a 36-hour washout when switching from sacubitril/valsartan.
Class effects to counsel on: dry cough, angioedema (higher risk in Black patients), hyperkalaemia, first-dose hypotension.
Beware the 'triple whammy' (ACE inhibitor + diuretic + NSAID) precipitating acute kidney injury.
Check potassium and renal function within 1-2 weeks of starting or increasing the dose.
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed one and continue your normal schedule - do not double up. If you miss several doses, contact your prescriber, as blood pressure may rise.
overdose: Overdose causes marked hypotension, shock, electrolyte disturbance (hyperkalaemia), bradycardia, and renal failure. Place the patient supine; treat hypotension with IV normal saline volume expansion, and consider catecholamines if needed. Angiotensin II infusion may be considered. Perindoprilat can be removed by haemodialysis. Monitor blood pressure, renal function, and serum potassium; treat hyperkalaemia and bradycardia symptomatically.
